_meta.description: Mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties for FDM materials with design limits. Includes brand-specific filament profiles with per-brand printing parameters. Agent-consumable — structured for constraint reasoning, not human reference.

_data_quality.update_cadence: annual for established materials (PLA, PETG, ABS), semi-annual for newer composites (CF-Nylon, PA6-GF, PET-CF); high-performance polymers (PEI, PEEK, PEKK, PPSU, PPS) annual — their datasheets change rarely, but vendor process windows do
_data_quality.methodology: Conservative/worst-case values used for composites where manufacturer specs vary. Mechanical values represent typical FDM-printed properties (not injection-molded datasheets). Design limits empirically validated where possible.

_meta._split_note: Safety-floor profiles for AI-controlled FDM printing.  Engineering-grade properties (mechanical, design limits, use-case ratings, brand tuning, curated guidance) are available in Kiln Pro.  See https://kiln3d.com/pricing.

chemical.handling_warning: Processed at 380-450C, far above commodity filaments. Supplier safety documentation for this family recommends local exhaust ventilation, and thermal decomposition products are hazardous to inhale. No supplier publishes quantitative fume, VOC or ultrafine-particle emission rates, so ventilate on principle rather than to a measured limit. Parts also leave the chamber hot enough to burn.
chemical.uv_note: Direct sun yellows it heavily and costs it most of its stretch, while strength and stiffness barely move — a static strength check will not catch it. Paint or pigment anything staying outdoors.

chemical.esd_band_reference: ANSI/ESD S541 classifies a static-dissipative material as a surface or volume resistance of at least 1.0e4 and under 1.0e11 ohms. Note the unit: S541 moved off resistivity (ohms/square, ohm-cm) to resistance (ohms) in 2003, so a datasheet quoting ohms/square is not quoting the quantity the standard classifies, and the conversion factor between them depends on the test fixture's electrode geometry.
chemical.esd_grounding_note: A dissipative part only works if charge has somewhere to go. ANSI/ESD S20.20 requires a worksurface to measure under 1.0e9 ohms both across itself and from itself to ground; meeting only the first is not compliance. A fixture with no bonding feature is a resistor, not a drain.
chemical.esd_charge_generation_note: Being dissipative controls how charge LEAVES the part. It says nothing about whether the part GENERATES charge -- ANSI/ESD S541 states plainly that there is no correlation between resistance and low-charging behaviour, and no ANSI-approved pass/fail triboelectric test for a material exists, so this property cannot be certified by any vendor.
chemical.esd_qualification_note: The number on a spool describes the filament, not your part. Printed resistance moves with nozzle temperature, layer height, wall count and build orientation, and it is measurably worse across the layers than along them. Qualify a coupon printed with your production settings on your production machine; a datasheet value narrows the candidate list, it does not qualify the part.
chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: Resistance falls as nozzle temperature rises -- roughly three decades across a 40C window, documented independently by three compounders. One anchor grade drops below 1.0e4 ohms at 290C, which is out of the dissipative band and into the CONDUCTIVE one. Running hotter for better layer adhesion can therefore cost you the ESD classification in the direction nobody warns about, and a floating conductive fixture can dump charge into a device in a single fast discharge. Pick a temperature, qualify at it, and hold it.
chemical.service_temp_note: 60C is a continuous service temperature published by one vendor against IEC 60216. Most vendors publish none at all. Heat-deflection figures for this family sit around 65-76C at 0.45 MPa, which is a short-term deflection test and not a service rating.

design_limits.min_wall_thickness_note: 1.5 mm is an ESD floor, not a strength floor. A vendor on this platform specifies a 1.5 mm minimum wall for the electrical property as well as for interlayer bonding -- thin walls degrade dissipation, not just stiffness.

chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: One industrial vendor tested this material class across geometries and orientations per ANSI/ESD S20.20, S11.11 and STM11.12 and measured a five-decade spread (1.0e4 to 1.0e9 ohms), with extra variability on thin-walled cylinders. That spread is the honest picture of a printed part; a compound specification is not.
chemical.service_temp_note: 80C is published by a single vendor against IEC 60216 and is the only continuous service temperature published for this material anywhere. One vendor explicitly prints N/A rather than claim one. It sits about 20-25C below the 100-107C glass transition, a normal derate. Do not push toward 90C for load-bearing or dimensionally critical fixtures -- that is within about 10C of heat deflection.
chemical.handling_warning: Styrene-family material printed hot in a closed chamber. Ventilate the working area. Enclosure is not optional here: a warped tray does not sit flat under a board, which is the entire reason the tray exists.

chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: This is the clearest published case of resistance being a process variable rather than a material constant. At a fixed 280C nozzle, part orientation alone moves the published figure about two decades. Across 280-320C it moves about four. A part printed hot enough to bond well can land in the CONDUCTIVE band, which for a fixture in contact with a device is its own hazard, not a bonus.
chemical.service_temp_note: No vendor publishes a continuous service temperature for this material. 125C is the heat-deflection figure at 1.8 MPa, the conservative of the two published loads, used here as a load-bearing proxy. The widely quoted 157C is the SAME test at 0.45 MPa and is not a service rating. Both sit far above the 41.8C glass transition -- this polymer is semi-crystalline so it serves above Tg, but stiffness and creep resistance fall away well before either deflection figure.
chemical.moisture_note: Absorbs moisture readily and it costs real strength: the vendor publishes a wet set of mechanical values alongside the dry set, and in-plane tensile drops about 13 percent at 4.6 percent moisture content. Dry hard and keep it dry. The vendor wants a heated dryer feeding the printer DURING the build, not only before it. No vendor publishes how moisture affects the electrical property.

chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: This grade extrudes near 295C, the hottest of the static-dissipative materials, and these compounds get more conductive the hotter they are run. The gap between a temperature that welds layers well and one that walks the part out of the dissipative band is narrower here than on the lower-temperature grades. Fix a temperature, qualify a part at it, and hold it.
chemical.service_temp_note: No vendor publishes a continuous service temperature for this material. The 115C figure is not a published value: it carries the same margin below glass transition that the unfilled polycarbonate record uses, and is rounded down. The published 135C is heat deflection at the lighter 0.45 MPa load, which is a short-term test and not a service rating; no figure is published at the heavier load at all.
chemical.handling_warning: Processed near 295C in a closed hot chamber. Ventilate the working area, and expect parts to leave the chamber hot enough to burn. Drying needs 120C, above what an ordinary filament dryer reaches.

chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: The vendor states outright that this compound's resistance can be tuned by extruder temperature. That makes the electrical property a process output rather than something delivered on the spool. Fix an extruder temperature, qualify a part printed at it, and re-qualify whenever the profile changes.
chemical.flame_rating_note: This grade publishes NO flame or fire-smoke-toxicity rating. The certified fire performance associated with this polymer family belongs to a different grade and to the unfilled resin, and such certification is awarded to a part at a thickness by an approved laboratory, not to a filament. Carbon loading changes burn behaviour. Do not assume this material carries a fire rating; if a programme requires one, it must be tested on the actual printed part.
chemical.service_temp_note: No vendor publishes a continuous service temperature. The 170C figure is derived, not measured: it carries a conservative margin below the 217C glass transition. The published 205C is heat deflection at the lighter 0.45 MPa load, a short-term test rather than a service rating, and no figure is published at the heavier load.
chemical.handling_warning: Extruded near 390C, far above commodity filaments. Ventilate; thermal decomposition products of this polymer family are hazardous to inhale, and parts leave the machine hot enough to burn.

chemical.esd_process_sensitivity_note: Orientation matters more on this material than on any other dissipative grade. Measured data shows resistance markedly worse across the layers than along them, and the carbon-fibre version of this material measures a full decade worse when printed upright. On a grade already specified near the insulative end, that penalty is enough to take a vertically printed face out of the dissipative band entirely -- while the part still looks correct and a flat test coupon still passes. Print faces that must dissipate FLAT.
chemical.sustained_load_note: No vendor in this material class publishes any creep data. This polymer creeps measurably at room temperature under sustained load, and creep accelerates as it approaches its 60C glass transition. A fixture's job is holding dimension under load for months, so the property that governs its actual duty is uncharacterised. The failure is silent drift out of tolerance rather than a visible crack. Do not use this material for a permanently clamped or loaded fixture.
chemical.annealing_note: Do not anneal a static-dissipative part. Annealing is the usual remedy for this polymer's low heat resistance, but the published literature indicates annealing conductive composites reduces conductivity by breaking down the percolation pathways that make the material dissipative, and no vendor has measured the effect on these grades. The mechanical fix plausibly breaks the electrical function.
chemical.service_temp_note: 40C is a deliberately conservative working figure, not a published one -- no vendor publishes a continuous service temperature. Heat deflection is 55C at the lighter 0.45 MPa load and glass transition is 60C, so a bench near an oven, a sunlit workshop or a closed vehicle consumes the margin. This is the least thermally capable static-dissipative material available.

chemical.orientation_note: Orientation matters more on this material than on any other dissipative grade. Between the two published build directions, tensile strength falls to about 59 percent and unnotched impact falls by a factor of thirty, while stiffness does not fall at all. A deflection check will look correct in both directions and will not reveal either loss.
chemical.service_temp_note: 150C is a conservative working figure below the 157.6C glass transition; no vendor publishes a continuous service temperature for a dissipative grade of this polymer. The heat-deflection data is unusually trustworthy: measured on printed parts, barely moving between the light and heavy test loads, and higher printed than moulded.
